places.name: タンメン ニュータマヤ (Tanmen New Tamaya)
places.neighborhood: Chikaramachi, Higashi Ward / Higashi-ōte Station area

noodles.notes: Thin, straight, and an oddly beautiful colour — one Nagoya blogger fixed on the yellow-to-beige cast, somewhere between kansui gold and raw dough, and on how much wheat you can smell in them. They are cut fine enough to be a surprise under a topping load this heavy, and they hold their bite to the bottom of the bowl. Supplier and hydration are not published.

ramen.signature_bowl: 大陸タンメン (Continental Tanmen, ¥800; ¥1,221 large) — the house salt tanmen with a ladle of owner Yukio Morishita's hand-made mapo tofu dropped on top, and dropped there deliberately unseasoned so you build the heat yourself from the table sansho. The plain タンメン, 味噌タンメン and 辛味タンメン all sit at ¥700, the ワイルド versions add karaage and gyoza, and the vegetable/oil/garlic call is free up to 全マシ.
ramen.chashu: There isn't one, and that is the point — a tanmen shop puts its pork in the wok, not on a braising rack. Sliced belly (バラ肉) goes into the pan with the vegetables and comes out lacquered in the same fond, so the meat reads as part of the stir-fry rather than a separate ceremony. The Continental adds a second, minced-pork layer inside the mapo tofu.
notable_toppings: free extra vegetables / oil / garlic, Jiro-style call
table sansho for the numbing finish

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles, wheat-brewed soy and doubanjiang in the mapo — one wok, no allergen protocol.

vegan.note: Chicken-bone stock carrying pork and seafood umami, with pork belly stir-fried into every bowl.

ramen.pantheon: Tanmen is not ramen's descendant so much as its sibling from the Chinese town-diner side of the family: no dark shoyu, no braised chashu, just a salt soup that takes its sweetness from a wok-load of vegetables seared hard and then flooded with stock. That searing is the whole soul — the sugars catch on cabbage and beansprouts, the pan's oil carries the smell into the bowl, and what you taste is a clean chicken-salt broth with a smoky vegetable sweetness laid over it and a slick of wok fat on top. New Tamaya then pushes the form somewhere Nagoya otherwise can't go: locals openly treat it as the city's stand-in for the mapo-topped Mōko Tanmen Nakamoto it lacks, right down to the free 野菜・油・にんにく call. Order the Continental and it arrives almost bland by design, a blank spicy canvas; you season it yourself, and the sansho at the end turns a comfort bowl numbing. Morishita's Instagram line is that he chases 唯一無二の至高のタンメン, a one-of-a-kind supreme tanmen, and the daily office-district queue suggests the neighbourhood agrees.

places.name: 担々麺専門店 麺屋•高豚 浄心店 (Tantanmen Senmonten Menya Haiton Joshin-ten)
places.neighborhood: Jōshin (Nishi-ku)

noodles.notes: Straight noodles, which the group's regulars say 絡む — grip — unusually well for a straight cut, because the sesame-thickened soup coats rather than runs off. The brothless 担々まぜそば is built on the same principle and reviewers single out how completely the sauce clings. No maker, gauge or hydration has been published for this branch.

ramen.signature_bowl: とんこつ担々麺 — the group's creamy pork-bone soup rebuilt as a sesame-and-chili tantanmen, and then broken open by the house move: 厚切りチャーシュー, thick-cut chashu slabs, laid on in place of the ground pork every other tantanmen uses. The brothless 担々まぜそば is the other pillar. Opened 18 April 2025 in the basement of the Lumia Eleven building as the group's third shop and its first dedicated to tantanmen; lunch (11:30–14:00) comes with free rice, which is the correct vehicle for what the chashu leaves behind.
ramen.chashu: The reason the group has a following. Pork chashu cut in slabs rather than slices — 厚切り, thick enough that reviewers talk about 食べ応え, chew and heft — carried over from the parent shop's tonkotsu shoyu bowl where it is the entire selling point. Putting it on a tantanmen replaces the genre's soft mince with something you have to work at, which changes the bowl's whole rhythm.
notable_toppings: Sichuan pepper (sanshō) — the parent shop's tantanmen is praised for the numbing edge
counter jars of gyofun, garlic and doubanjiang for mid-bowl adjustment at the parent shop

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles; the sesame tare starts from wheat-brewed soy, and doubanjiang usually carries wheat too.

vegan.note: Hard-boiled pork-bone paitan, and the bowl's identity is its pork chashu.

ramen.pantheon: Japanese tantanmen long ago parted company with Sichuan dandan noodles: where the Chinese original is a small brothless bowl whose job is numbing heat, the Japanese one grew a soup, thickened it with sesame paste and rounded off the 花椒 for local palates. Haiton takes that already-domesticated bowl and drags it one step further from the ancestor by using its own tonkotsu as the carrier — so the sesame is riding a hard-boiled pork paitan rather than the usual light chicken stock, and the first mouthful lands thick, nutty and faintly sweet before the chili opens up behind it. Then it abandons the last convention. The mince goes; slabs of thick-cut chashu arrive; a spice bowl becomes a meat bowl, and the sesame's sweetness turns into a foil for pork fat instead of the main event. That the group opened a whole shop for this — plus the brothless 担々まぜそば version — is very Nagoya: this is the city that decided noodles are better mixed than soaked.

places.name: 拉麺しま (Ramen Shima)
places.neighborhood: Jōshin (Nishi-ku)

noodles.notes: 細麺ストレート — thin and straight, the default cut of the old chuka soba trade, chosen to be carried by a soup this light rather than to fight one. Nothing about the maker or hydration is published.

ramen.signature_bowl: 拉麺, ¥500 including tax, ¥700 for the large — in 2026 very likely the cheapest genuine ramen bowl in Nagoya. Local write-ups reach for 素朴 (plain) and 懐かしい (nostalgic) and describe the soup as お湯割り系: thin, deliberately dilute, the opposite of the concentration race. The toppings are said to be generous for what you pay. Which stock the shop actually simmers has never been written down anywhere.
ramen.chashu: Undocumented. Reviewers say the bowl is well-loaded for ¥500 but nobody has described the cut or the treatment; expect the conventional rolled-and-braised chuka soba chashu of the genre until someone reports otherwise.
notable_toppings: reported only as 具もしっかり — generous for the price; the individual garnishes have never been itemised

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles in a wheat-brewed shoyu soup; a bare ¥500 counter with no allergen handling.

vegan.note: Stock undocumented, but a ¥500 chuka soba runs on animal bones and the bowl comes with chashu.

ramen.pantheon: This is the survival of a genre Japan has mostly priced out of existence: the neighbourhood 拉麺 counter where the soup is thin, salty, cheap and completely unembarrassed about it. Reviewers reach for the same word every time — 懐かしい — because the broth is dilute by intent rather than by failure, the light shoyu chuka soba that fed Showa factory shifts long before koku became a competitive sport. There is no branded chicken, no aroma oil, no lineage claim, no story: just a fine straight noodle in a modest soup, priced at what a coffee costs. Read against the ¥1,500 jidori bowls a few stations away it is almost an argument — a reminder that for most of ramen's life the point was that anyone could afford dinner. The shop's own sign is an A4 sheet taped up beside the noren; find it on Jōhoku-chō, between Jōshin and Shōnai-dōri, and expect nothing to be explained to you.

places.name: 岩野屋 (Iwanoya)
places.neighborhood: Around Sengen-chō Station (~1.1 km from Nagoya Castle)

noodles.notes: Nothing is published. This is a soba/udon/kishimen kitchen first, so the chukamen is almost certainly bought in rather than cut in-house — but no one has confirmed even that.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば sits on the board beside kishimen, soba, niku udon, curry udon, miso nikomi udon and ankake noodles — the full all-rounder spread of a Showa-era Nagoya 麺類食堂 on the old Mino-ji road. No one has ever described the bowl itself: not the soup, not the noodle, not the toppings. Honest answer — come for the kishimen, and treat the chuka soba as an open question worth asking at the counter.

gf.note: Every noodle in the house is wheat, and the dashi runs on tamari and standard soy.

vegan.note: Nagoya menrui dashi is katsuobushi/muro-aji — fish is in every broth here, vegetable toppings included.

ramen.pantheon: The 中華そば on a Japanese soba shop's menu is a genre of its own, and a quietly interesting one: not a ramen specialist's bowl but the noodle-shop version, ladled from the same counter as the kishimen and usually seasoned in the same wafu register — bonito and tamari where a ramen-ya would reach for pork bone and kansui swagger. In Nagoya that register is unusually distinctive, because the local dashi tradition is muro-aji and dark tamari, which gives even a Chinese-style bowl a soba-shop soul. Iwanoya has kept a Showa room going on the old Mino-ji road for decades, five minutes from Sengen-chō and a short walk from Nagoya Castle, offering exactly the spread a working neighbourhood expects. Whether its chuka soba is a true animal-stock ramen or that wafu cousin is simply not on record — which is the honest state of a great many neighbourhood counters, and worth saying out loud rather than inventing around.

places.name: らぁ麺 藤花 (Ramen Toka)
places.neighborhood: Sengen-chō / Jōshin

noodles.notes: 自家製麺, milled in-house from a three-way Hokkaido wheat blend — ゆめちから (Yumechikara, high-protein backbone), 春よ恋 (Haruyokoi, aroma and elasticity) and きたほなみ (Kitahonami, softness and sweetness). The result is described as ツルッとしなやか: slippery and supple rather than aggressively firm, tuned to slide through a clear soup instead of standing up to a heavy one. The cut itself has not been published.

ramen.signature_bowl: 地鶏醤油らぁ麺, ¥950, with 上 at ¥1,210 and 特上 at ¥1,540; a shio runs alongside. The broth is drawn from branded jidori — Nagoya Cochin and Kyoto red chicken — then squared off with Rausu kombu, 白口煮干し (shirokuchi niboshi) and katsuobushi. The shoyu tare is a three-soy blend: Aichi tamari, Kagawa 生醤油 and Shimane 再仕込み. The shio tare goes the other way entirely, built on Kumejima salt and Setouchi moshio with scallop and clam behind it. The 特上 loads six pieces of chashu, kombu-cured chicken breast and house-made pork chips onto the same bowl.
ramen.chashu: Seto pork worked across the entire animal — loin, shoulder, rib, belly, tenderloin and rump — each cut given the treatment it deserves rather than one method applied to everything: sous-vide low-temperature cooking for the lean cuts, spit-roasting for others, braising for the rest. The premium tiers add kombu-jime chicken breast, cured rather than cooked, and crisp house-made pork chips for a third texture. The 特上 is effectively a chashu tasting flight served over soup.
notable_toppings: up to six pieces of multi-cut Seto pork chashu
windows facing Nagoya Castle's northwest turret

gf.note: Three wheat-brewed soy sauces in the tare and house-milled wheat noodles — no safe bowl here, despite the app's earlier 'ask'.

vegan.note: Jidori chicken broth reinforced with niboshi and katsuobushi, plus pork chashu.

ramen.pantheon: This is the modern 清湯 jidori shoyu bowl — the style that swept Japan's ramen awards through the 2010s and reframed ramen as something closer to French stock work: a broth clear enough to read the bottom of the bowl, meant to be sipped like consommé, with noodle and pork treated as separately sourced ingredients rather than accessories. Toka's soul is the bird. Nagoya Cochin and Kyoto red chicken give a jidori broth that lands savoury and clean rather than fatty, propped up by Rausu kombu, with the shirokuchi niboshi and katsuo arriving a beat later so the seafood reads as an aftertaste rather than a statement. The three-soy tare is the craft tell — tamari for depth and colour, nama-shoyu for fragrance, saishikomi for the dark sweetness behind it — the sort of blending a shop only bothers with when the broth is clear enough to expose the seasoning. The body is house-milled from three named Hokkaido wheats, supple by design. And the heart is unusually plural: six cuts of Seto pork, each cooked its own way, which is exactly why the 特上 is the bowl to spend on. Opened May 2024 by a husband-and-wife pair with no published pedigree, which makes the technical ambition here more impressive, not less.

places.name: 龍園 (Ryuen)
places.neighborhood: Jōshin (Nishi-ku)

noodles.notes: 自家製 中細麺 — house-made and medium-thin, with a chew reviewers keep singling out. That matters here: the soup is soft-spoken enough that a limp noodle would leave nothing to hold on to, and the koshi is what gives a 3 am bowl its structure.

ramen.signature_bowl: A plain ramen, about ¥800 — chicken bone and pork bone cut with soy, and 無化調, built without MSG. It comes out honestly cloudy and then drinks light, which is the paradox worth turning up for. And the way to eat it is not at the Kami-Nagoya shop at all: the owner wheels a ten-seat yatai out near Sanzō-dōri in Sumiyoshi-chō, opening around 2:00 am and running to roughly 7:00, closed Sundays, closed in the rain, and otherwise closed whenever he decides.
ramen.chashu: Pork chashu cut with the fat left generously on — 脂身多め, and reviewers mean that as praise. It is doing structural work: in a broth this restrained the melting fat is what supplies richness, so the chashu is less a topping than the bowl's second seasoning.

gf.note: House-made wheat-and-kansui noodles, wheat-brewed shoyu tare — 無化調 means no MSG, not no gluten.

vegan.note: Chicken- and pork-bone stock, with fatty pork chashu on top.

ramen.pantheon: The yatai is ramen's ancestral form of service — the cart, the ten stools, the soup that has to be good enough to sell at an hour when nobody is being discerning — and Nagoya has almost none of them left. Ryuen keeps one alive: the same owner who cooks at the Nishi-ku shop rolls out after two in the morning, weather and Sundays permitting, and serves a chicken-and-pork shoyu that is visibly cloudy yet drinks あっさり. That contradiction is the whole craft — a well-skimmed double stock emulsifies enough to turn opaque without ever going heavy, so the bowl looks like a commitment and eats like a kindness. Building it 無化調 changes the timing too: without MSG the savouriness unfolds slowly and rounds off instead of snapping at you, which is precisely what a body wants at 3 am, and it puts all the weight on the fat from the chashu to carry the finish. The house-made medium-thin noodle gives it spine. Regulars talk about finding the cart the way you'd talk about finding a mythical island — the hunt is half the bowl, and the not-knowing is the tradition.

noodles.notes: Two different noodles for two different soups, which is the tell of a kitchen that thinks in pairings. The shio takes 全粒粉入り細麺 — thin, straight, cut with whole-wheat flour so the grain flavour and the firm snap stand up against a gentle broth. The shoyu gets a thicker straight noodle (徳粉中太) with more body. Neither is wavy. Kaedama refills are ¥100.

ramen.signature_bowl: しおラーメン, ¥750–780 — poured clear enough to see the bottom of the bowl, and it reads as a fine wafu dashi before it reads as ramen. A ゆずしお option is +¥50 and worth it for the lift it puts on top of the fish. The しょうゆらーめん (¥680–700) is the thicker-noodled counterpart, a とんこつらーめん (¥680) rounds out the board, and the house 炊き込みご飯 at ¥200 is the local order alongside. Opened 8 January 2018 on a quiet residential lane near Asama-chō.
ramen.chashu: Two preparations run side by side and you choose: a conventional braised chashu, tender and firmly seasoned, or a low-temperature-cooked version with the rosy centre and softer, hammier texture that method gives. Extra portions about ¥200. Offering both on a menu this small is a statement — the shop wants you to notice that chashu is a technique, not an ingredient.
notable_toppings: house-made takikomi gohan on the side

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles — the shio's are cut with whole wheat — and both tare start from wheat-brewed soy.

vegan.note: Four-fish dashi blended with pork bone, plus pork chashu.

ramen.pantheon: Hiiragi sits on the gentle wing of the modern gyokai-tonkotsu double soup — the pairing that dominates contemporary Japanese ramen, but built here with the pork bone as a floor rather than a wall. Four 節 do the talking on top: katsuo, saba, muro-aji and sōda-bushi, the same fish quartet a serious soba shop would reach for, so the first thing to arrive is a clean dried-fish fragrance and only afterwards the animal underneath it. The shio is the shop's argument, and it is a chintan in the strict sense — gently simmered, never broken into cloudiness, transparent to the bottom. What makes it more than pretty is the counterweight: a whole-wheat thin noodle with real grain flavour and bite, deliberately given something to say in a soup that never raises its voice, and then a different, thicker noodle for the shoyu because that broth needs a different partner. Add the yuzu-shio and the bowl tilts almost into kaiseki territory. This is the neighbourhood hideaway version of high-technique ramen — warm wooden counter, sub-¥1,000 bowls, no fuss made about any of it.

places.neighborhood: 中区 丸の内 (Naka Ward, Marunouchi)

noodles.notes: Diners single the noodles out for praise — とっても美味しい — but no spec has ever been published: no gauge, no cut, no maker. Conventional wheat chukamen.

ramen.signature_bowl: The lunch board runs two tantanmen in parallel: 肉坦々麺, the meat version, which reviewers call ほんのり甘味もあってコク深い — faintly sweet with real depth — and ベジ坦々麺, a plant-based bowl the kitchen states outright is 動物性食材不使用. Side by side the vegan one drinks あっさり優しい, lighter and gentler, with sesame and chili doing the work the animal stock does in the other. The whole kitchen runs without chemical seasonings or refined sugar, on koji and natural salt instead.
ramen.chashu: None, by design. The vegan bowl's mince is 大豆ミート (soy meat), and in place of the seasoned egg it uses 麩 — baked wheat gluten, an old temple-kitchen substitution that soaks up sesame broth the way a chashu never could.
notable_toppings: fu (baked wheat gluten) standing in for the ajitama
yakuzen dinner courses alongside — herbal soup, clay-pot mapo tofu, yuba ankake chahan

gf.note: Wheat noodles, sesame-and-soy tare, and the signature vegan garnish is 麩 — pure baked wheat gluten.

vegan.note: The ベジ坦々麺 is stated by the restaurant as 動物性食材不使用, a standing lunch item rather than a special request; confirm the day's stock at the counter since the meat version shares the kitchen.

ramen.pantheon: Tantanmen cooked in a 薬膳 kitchen is a different animal from tantanmen cooked in a ramen shop. The goal is balance rather than impact — sesame for nourishment, chili for circulation — so nobody is chasing a numbing knockout, and the bowl is deliberately built without MSG or refined sugar, seasoned on koji and natural salt. That subtraction is what you taste: with no glutamate scaffolding, the sesame's own roasted nuttiness is left standing in the open, and the chili reads as warmth rather than assault. Chef Ai Hiroshi holds international certification as a 国際薬膳調理師 and cooked as a hotel head chef before opening this fifteen-seat husband-and-wife room in Marunouchi, and the two tantanmen are the clearest expression of the method — the meat bowl rounder and slightly sweet, the vegan one clean and softly savoury, the same architecture with the animal layer simply removed. For this app the vegan version is the genuinely rare thing: a fully animal-free noodle bowl on an ordinary Chinese lunch menu. And the fu standing in for the egg tells you how old this vegetarian technique is — and exactly why it remains off-limits to celiacs.

places.name: フジヤマ55 金シャチ横丁店 (Fujiyama 55 Kinshachi Yokocho)
places.neighborhood: Nagoya Castle, Kinshachi Yokochō Muneharu Zone, Shiyakusho Stn

noodles.notes: 自家製極太麺, cut fresh in-house every morning from three things only — flour, kansui and potato starch, with no preservatives and no humectants. The starch is the point: it gives the もちもち, mochi-like pull that a dip this thick demands, and a plain wheat noodle would go slack under it. The jiro-kei bowl takes a house-made flat noodle instead, and the group also runs a 自家製ちぢれ麺 crimped cut on its soup ramen.

ramen.signature_bowl: 濃厚つけ麺 (¥900, ¥960 large; all-topping ¥1,250) — the dip is a two-day build: day one is 80kg-plus of pork bone at a hard rolling boil, day two folds in whole chicken, and the pot is finished with aromatic vegetables and a katsuo/saba/aji seafood hit. RED chili versions are +¥30; shrimp (¥920) and beef-offal dips sit alongside. Finish it the way the shop intends — 追い飯, rice tipped into what's left of the dip to make an ojiya. The 台湾まぜそば (¥950, free rice refill) is the other reason to come, and this branch has a location-exclusive Sakura Mazesoba at the same price. Jiro-kei ramen is ¥800, miso jiro ¥850.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork, and measured in impact rather than finesse — two-slice top-ups run ¥110–¥220 and the 全部のせ builds bury the bowl. On the jiro-kei ramen it is the blunt slab beneath the beansprout-and-cabbage mound, doing exactly the job Jiro lineage asks of it. This is a chain that treats pork as volume, not as a tasting exercise, and is entirely unapologetic about that.
notable_toppings: beansprouts and cabbage on the jiro-kei bowl
spiced Taiwan mince on the mazesoba
free rice refill with the mazesoba
追い飯 to close the tsukemen

gf.note: House-cut wheat noodles and a wheat-brewed shoyu dip; the miso jiro may add barley or wheat miso.

vegan.note: Pork bone plus whole chicken, finished with katsuo, saba and aji; the mazesoba's core topping is pork mince.

ramen.pantheon: Fujiyama 55 is Nagoya's home-grown answer to Tokyo's gyokai-tonkotsu tsukemen boom. Ryuichiro Sawa — born in Nagoya in 1971, five years in a corporate job before he opened Chūka Soba Tsurumai Ikkokuya — met tsukemen while touring Japan's ramen, brought it home to Ōsu in 1997, and grew it to roughly seventy shops. The soul is that two-day pot: bones smashed at a hard boil until the collagen breaks into the water, whole chicken folded in on the second day for sweetness and body, then the whole opaque thing cracked open with three dried fish. What lands is thick, gelatinous pork depth followed immediately by a sharp seafood top note — the one-two that defines the genre and the reason the dip has to be this concentrated to survive contact with cold noodles. The body is unusually literal here: extra-thick, starch-boosted, cut that morning, built for grabbing a sauce that clings rather than for slurping a soup. And the Kinshachi Yokochō branch sets that beside 台湾まぜそば, the brothless spiced-mince bowl Nagoya invented in 2008 and now exports nationwide — mix it hard, then close with the free rice. The through-line of the whole shop is that second act: 追い飯 on the tsukemen, 追い飯 on the mazesoba. In Nagoya you are meant to eat the bowl twice.

noodles.notes: Flat-cut noodles (平打ち麺) developed jointly with the Nagoya ramen shop 俺の豚骨 (Ore no Tonkotsu) rather than made in-house — mochi-mochi springy, cut wide so a thin soup has surface to cling to. This is the one part of the bowl a specialist touched, and it shows: the body of the ramen is more serious than its soul. Hydration and maker are unpublished.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (chuka soba, ¥990) — pale soy soup with じんわりとした優しい旨味, a savouriness that arrives slowly rather than hitting, over wide flat noodles and dressed in the full Showa uniform: chashu, menma, negi, narutomaki, nori. It is not the house flagship. Noma-san built the shop around 町中華オムライス (¥1,320) — town-Chinese omurice — and the chuka soba is its noodle counterpart on a deliberately short opening menu, with more dishes promised as the kitchen finds its feet.
ramen.chashu: Sliced pork chashu in the plain machi-chuka manner — braised, thin-cut, laid flat over the noodles as one element among five rather than the centrepiece. The shop has published nothing about the cut or the braise and no reviewer has pressed the point; in this genre the chashu is expected to be modest, and it is.

gf.note: Wheat noodles and a wheat-brewed soy tare; no gluten-free option and no allergen protocol in a 12-seat shared-wok kitchen.

vegan.note: Animal stock, pork chashu, and a shared wok line. No plant-based bowl.

ramen.pantheon: This is the humblest register in ramen — the 中華そば of a 町中華, the soup a Chinese-restaurant cook ladles out between orders of fried rice, and the bowl a generation of Nagoya office workers grew up eating without ever calling it ramen. Noma-san came to cooking at forty after a career selling electrical equipment, trained around Nagoya's Chinese kitchens, and what he opened in December 2025 is that unglamorous lineage played completely straight: no oil cap, no fashion, nothing to prove, just a gently sweet soy broth and the naruto-and-nori dress code that dates the style to the Showa era. The soul is undemonstrative on purpose — machi-chuka soup is meant to be drinkable at the end of a shift, not stared at. Note that the kitchen has published nothing about its stock, so the chicken-chintan reading here is inference from tasting notes, not fact.

places.name: 濃厚中華そば 佐とう (Noko Chuka Soba Sato)
places.neighborhood: Naka-ku, Marunouchi / 3 min walk from Marunouchi Stn

noodles.notes: Medium-thin straight noodles with a hard, snapping bite — reviewers reach for ポキポキ, the word for something that breaks rather than yields. That is a low-hydration cut doing exactly the job it should: a soup this concentrated will invade any noodle that lets it in, so this one is built dry and stiff and stays defined to the last mouthful. Maker unpublished; the shop makes no jikasei-men claim.

ramen.signature_bowl: 濃厚中華そば (roughly ¥830–930) — a near-black bowl of tamari-soy broth carrying seafood umami and a heavy slick of scorched garlic oil, under a fan of paper-thin pork belly that covers the entire surface. The menu is deliberately tiny and the presentation austere: chashu, thick-cut white negi, nothing else. Kombu vinegar and black pepper sit on the tables, and by the halfway mark you will want them — the vinegar is the intended release valve, not an afterthought.
ramen.chashu: Pork belly, braised soft and shaved so thin it drapes, then piled in enough slices to hide the noodles entirely. This is the shop's inheritance made visible: before the pivot to ramen in October 2018 the owner ran a donburi restaurant, Le Granbowl, at the same address, and the meat handling came with him. The trick is volume without weight — it reads like an extravagant amount of pork and eats light because no single slice has any thickness to it.
notable_toppings: thin-sliced pork belly chashu, piled to cover the bowl
paper aprons handed out on request

gf.note: Wheat noodles. The tare is tamari shoyu, which in Aichi is soybean-dominant, but the shop makes no gluten-free claim and the noodles rule the bowl out regardless.

vegan.note: Pork belly chashu over a seafood-and-animal stock; nothing plant-based on the menu.

ramen.pantheon: The soul of this bowl is Aichi's own soy sauce. Tamari — thick, almost black, brewed from soybeans with little or no wheat, the condiment that makes Tokai cooking taste like Tokai — is normally used as a finishing dab on sashimi, and Sato builds an entire ramen on it, taking Nakagawa Jozo's tamari and refusing to blend it into politeness. What arrives looks like engine oil and drinks far easier than it looks: seafood umami underneath, a bitter-edged burnt-garlic oil floating on top, a tare concentrated enough that the shop keeps paper aprons behind the counter. Not every palate survives it — one careful reviewer found the garlic one-dimensional by the bottom of the bowl — and the honest reading is that this is a bowl with a single enormous idea rather than a balanced one. That is also why there is a queue outside a Marunouchi office block at 11am, six years running.

places.name: 楽いち (Rakuichi)
places.neighborhood: Meijō Park / Nishi-ku, Kaminagoya (~8 min walk from Meijō Kōen Stn)

noodles.notes: Thin straight noodles are the house default and the thing regulars single out first — 細麺 is a Kyushu instinct and something of an outlier in Nagoya, where thicker cuts dominate. A medium gauge can be requested instead. Supplier and hydration undocumented.

ramen.signature_bowl: 楽いち味 ("the Rakuichi flavour", roughly ¥800–1,000) — the house pork-bone bowl, lifted by shima-tougarashi, the small fierce island chili of Okinawa, rather than by fat. Extra negi and a spoonful of kara-miso are the standard modifications; most regulars pair it with the chashu-don or the minced-pork rice as a set, sometimes for ¥50 off. Ten counter seats, one man cooking, evenings belong to regulars ordering beer alongside the bowl.
ramen.chashu: Pork chashu, tender and generously cut, doing double duty as the topping for the shop's chashu-don. It is the reason the rice sets sell: the same meat that sits on the noodles is what people come back for on rice. The shop publishes nothing about the cut or whether it is braised or seared.

gf.note: Wheat noodles and a wheat-brewed soy tare; no gluten-free noodle and no allergen policy at a one-man counter.

vegan.note: Pork-bone broth, pork chashu, pork rice sides. Nothing plant-based.

ramen.pantheon: A pork-bone bowl that refuses to be heavy. Tonkotsu's entire reputation rests on the violence of the boil — bones hammered for hours until fat and collagen emulsify into that opaque white soup — and Rakuichi keeps the pork soul while pulling the volume right down, to the point where regulars argue over whether it is あっさり or the made-up middle word こっさり: light on the tongue, still deep underneath. Anyone arriving expecting Hakata will find it thin; anyone tired of Hakata will find it exactly right. The heat is the shop's signature and it comes from chili, not fat — shima-tougarashi gives a dry, bright sting that lifts the pork instead of coating it, and the thin straight noodle is the correct body for a soup that never gets viscous. A residential side street near Meijo Park, ten seats, no press: the documentation is genuinely thin here and this reading should be treated as provisional.

places.name: 焼鳥 あらい (Yakitori Arai)
places.neighborhood: 浅間町 (Asama-cho), 西区, 名古屋

places.name: 中華そば 白壁 あおい (Chuka Soba Shirakabe Aoi)
places.neighborhood: Higashi-ōte Stn / Shirakabe / northeast of Nagoya Castle

noodles.notes: 自家製中細縮れ麺 — house-made medium-thin crimped noodles, cut fresh daily. This is the Takayama signature and a genuine technical oddity: low-hydration dough (the style runs around 28–32%) is stiff and resists crimping, so almost nobody else in Japan makes a noodle both dry and strongly wavy. The point is twofold — the crimp gives a low-fat soup something to cling to, and the dry noodle then drinks that soup into itself, which is where the style's famous 一体感, soup-and-noodle-as-one-thing, comes from.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (roughly ¥800–900; the loaded 全部のせ around ¥1,000) — dark-looking soy broth that tastes nothing like it looks, over house-made crimped noodles, with pork chashu braised to collapse, thick crisp menma and a soft-centred ajitama. The first thing you get is a puff of katsuo, then vegetable sweetness. Miso soba (¥900), 焼豚そば (¥900) and a mazesoba (¥950) were added later, but the Takayama bowl is the shop's reason to exist; lunch comes with free rice, which locals use to mop the last of the broth.
ramen.chashu: Pork braised to the point of collapse — ホロっと, meaning it comes apart under the chopsticks rather than holding as a slice. That softness is deliberate against a soup carrying almost no fat of its own: the chashu supplies the richness the broth declines to. A dedicated 焼豚そば is on the menu for anyone who wants the meat to lead the bowl instead of supporting it.
notable_toppings: thick-cut menma, assertively seasoned yet soft
ajitsuke tamago with a silky yolk

gf.note: Wheat noodles, and the wheat-brewed soy tare is boiled through the whole stockpot — there is no unseasoned soup here at all.

vegan.note: Chicken, pork and beef stock with a katsuo dashi note, plus pork chashu and a marinated egg.

ramen.pantheon: A Hida-Takayama bowl transplanted 150km south, and one of Japan's genuine structural oddities. Everywhere else in ramen, broth and tare are kept apart on purpose, so one pot of soup can yield shoyu, shio or miso by swapping the seasoning at the last second. Takayama refuses the split: the soy tare goes into the zundo and simmers with the stock, which is why Hida chuka soba comes in exactly one flavour and can never come in another. What that produces is a soup that looks dark and reads gentle — chicken and pork bones with beef and a heap of aromatic onion, a bonito lift on the first sip, almost no fat on the surface, a sweetness that is vegetable rather than sugared. A low-fat soup should feel thin, and this one does not, because the body rescues it: dry, strongly crimped noodles that grip the broth and then absorb it. Ryuichiro Sawa inherited this counter from his parents at 35 and went on to build the 59-shop Fujiyama 55 tsukemen chain out of it — the empire is elsewhere, but the family recipe, and the repeated pilgrimages he made up to Takayama to get it honest, are here.

noodles.notes: Thin noodles chosen for のどごし — the slippery throat-feel that a low-oil salt broth wants, since there is no fat to carry the noodle down. Cut, hydration and maker are unpublished.

ramen.signature_bowl: 鶏レモンラーメン (chicken lemon ramen, ¥870) — a clear chicken-and-salt soup laid with overlapping lemon slices and a nest of shiraga-negi, with chicken chashu in place of pork so the whole bowl stays on one animal and nothing muddies the citrus. The oil content is low enough that regulars finish the soup without guilt. The counter runs two stocks side by side, the chicken chuka-soba base and a tonkotsu, so the same twenty-seat room serves the brightest bowl in the neighbourhood and its opposite; gyoza and chashu-don fill out the sides, and lunch sets come with rice and pickles.
ramen.chashu: Chicken chashu, not pork — cooked until it crumbles at the touch of the chopsticks, lean and seasoned lightly so it never fights the lemon. Choosing bird over pig here is a structural decision, not a health one: pork fat and citrus argue, and the bowl is built to keep them apart. The tonkotsu side of the menu reverts to conventional pork chashu.
notable_toppings: sliced lemon laid across the surface
gyoza and chashu rice bowls alongside
lunch sets with rice and pickles

gf.note: Wheat noodles, a soy-and-dashi based tare, and gyoza wrappers in a small shared kitchen. No gluten-free option.

vegan.note: Both house stocks are animal — chicken bone and pork bone — and the bowl is finished with chicken chashu.

ramen.pantheon: Lemon ramen is a recent Japanese fashion rather than an inherited regional style, and it earns its place by inverting the usual method: instead of building depth out of fat, it strips the oil away and lets acid and aroma do the carrying. The soul is a clear chicken chintan under a shio tare — the most exposed construction in all of ramen, because there is no fat cap and no dark soy to hide behind, and a stock that is anything less than clean will announce itself immediately. Here it holds. The lemon perfumes every lift of the noodles rather than souring the soup, the shiraga-negi adds a raw allium edge, and the chicken chashu keeps the bowl monochrome in the best sense. Open since June 2013 on a quiet Higashi-ku street, with the tonkotsu pot waiting on the other side of the menu for the nights when you want the exact opposite.
